# Course Overview {.unnumbered}

| Task | Question it answers |
|---|---|
| Run a tool (BLAST, an assembler, a clustering package) | What did the software return? |
| Explain the tool | What mathematical object and what algorithm is it using? |
| Design a small version of the tool | What assumptions does the method need, and where do they fail? |

This course is the second and third rows. Each lesson is one class meeting. It takes one kind of biological data, writes it as a mathematical object, states a precise problem and the assumptions that make it solvable, and then gives the algorithm, a worked example small enough to check by hand, and the cases where the assumptions fail. The lessons build small versions of real methods because a small implementation exposes the recurrence, graph, likelihood, or matrix operation that the full tool relies on.

::: {.timeline-table}
| Week | Lessons | Topics |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1–2 | A first sequence-comparison problem; scores as log-odds models |
| 2 | 3–4 | Recurrences and tables; global alignment, correctness, traceback |
| 3 | 5–6 | Local alignment; affine gaps; seed-and-extend search |
| 4 | 7–8 | Reads, k-mers, de Bruijn graphs; Eulerian paths, repeats, errors |
| 5 | Midterm 1, 9 | Probability and Markov chains for sequences |
| 6 | 10–11 | CpG islands as likelihood ratios; hidden Markov models |
| 7 | 12–13 | Viterbi; forward–backward and posterior decoding |
| 8 | 14–15 | Distances and UPGMA; parsimony and Fitch's algorithm |
| 9 | — | Spring break |
| 10 | Midterm 2, 16 | Expression matrices and PCA through the SVD |
| 11 | 17–18 | PCA in practice; multiple testing and FDR |
| 12 | 19–20 | Clustering and neighborhood graphs; embeddings and single-cell data |
| 13 | 21–22 | ODEs for gene regulation; Hill functions and the toggle switch |
| 14 | 23, workshop | Choosing a method; project workshop |
| 15 | 24, work session | Modern frontiers; final project work session |
:::
